doc.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

chapter: Free jazz, time and the Creative Music Studio
title: Time and propulsion in free jazz; phrasing and the blues
summary: Berger discusses European factions that forbid time, Rashied Ali, Blackwell and Ornette following phrases not bars, and blues singers such as Sonny Boy Williamson at the Heidelberg club.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That being in the moment, I know you both have talked about that. When you’re doing — let me rephrase — I saw a couple of things in your Columbia interview that I felt were important.

And you said the relationship of rhythm and playing with a rhythm in free jazz sometimes is controversial. Like was it, you said in Berlin if you were playing free jazz you weren’t supposed to be playing steady time?

Yeah. There are factions of free jazz movements, particularly actually in Europe and not so much here, that insisted that time was sort of out of the question, like you would not go there. And that’s still the case. There’s a few free jazz festivals in Europe where you cannot play time, like they would like pull you. And in America nobody quite thinks like that. Even Albert Ayler didn’t think that way. You know, like they just think of movement and you can play that in time, out of time, but there has to be that movement, you know, that propulsion that defines what jazz is all about. And that can be generated in multiple ways. Like I played a lot with Rashied Ali and he was like playing four times at the same time, you know, that kind of approach. It would move, but the whole thing was that the train has to be going. No matter how you do it. And I play a lot of — Blackwell was basically a traditional player in a lot of ways. Like he played time always. But he played time that you would not count two measures. So it’s not measured time. Like you don’t play four or five or three. But he would just play one-one-one-one-one, and depending where the phrase falls, there would be the one. You hear that in Ornette’s music all the time, right? Follow the phrase. And that’s not really only a jazz
phenomenon by the way. I mean The Beatles wrote songs and they followed the words. Like there are some words that just fall on five and then the beat is there. Which is the blues too you know.
Yeah, early blues is like that. And even famous blues guys like —

John Lee Hooker, you’d hear that all the time. And I remember way early on in that club in Heidelberg there was a concert series coming through called — it was sort of a blues, it was like a tour that Norman Granz did I think.

He had like some Chicago guys and then some from the south. And even in our club they were fighting over whether the blues got 12 bars or not. Sonny Boy Williamson was there. And he would say, “the blues is where the words are and that’s the form of the blues.” You know? Wherever the words go. It could be 12-1/2 or 11-1/2 or 13 or whatever. You just have to listen to the words. The words were more important. And this is with Charlie a little bit too. Like he writes, he sings, and depending on how he phrases the last word will be another half a bar or not.

That’s why I’m saying, like Blackwell for example, he comes from New Orleans. And in the south there’s just much less of an idea of bars. So no, they really think more in terms of phrasing words. And so Ornette’s music is like that you know? He doesn’t count bars. There is no bars.
As a schooled musician, can you do that on purpose?
